# Switching circuits and logic gates (`logic_gates_switching`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs boolean_logic, electromagnetism; helped by binary_numbers, electric_telegraph, vacuum_tube, semiconductors_transistor
- Core idea: Boolean logic can be built from switches. Two switches in series pass current only if both are closed (AND); two in parallel if either is closed (OR); a relay contact that opens when its coil is energised gives NOT. A relay is an electromagnet that works a switch, so the output of one circuit can drive the inputs of others. From these gates one builds a binary adder (the sum digit is 'one or the other but not both', the carry is 'both') and a memory element: two relays or valves, each holding the other in its state, stay as they were set (flip-flop) and store one binary digit. Any design can be written and simplified as Boolean algebra before a single part is wired.
- Pitfalls:
  - Overlooking earlier relay algebra. Nakashima published methods for telephone switching before Shannon’s thesis
  - Ignoring timing: contacts bounce and signals arrive at different moments, which gives false pulses unless the design allows for contact bounce and propagation delays
  - Loading one output with too many inputs, so that the signal is too weak to switch them
  - Thinking the principle depends on the device; relays, valves and transistors only differ in speed, size and reliability
- History: europe: 1918 – Eccles and Jordan's valve flip-flop (London); 1930 Bothe and Rossi describe electronic coincidence circuits. Shestakov recorded his relay algebra in 1935, defended his Moscow thesis in 1938 and published in 1941. In 1941 Zuse completed the relay-based Z3 in Berlin; east_asia: 1934–1936 – Akira Nakashima at NEC publishes a theory of relay circuits equivalent to two-valued Boolean algebra; americas: 1886 – Peirce's letter describing logic by switches; 1937 Shannon's master's thesis at MIT, published 1938; 1937 Stibitz's relay adder at Bell Labs
- Read:
  - Claude E. Shannon, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, Transactions of the AIEE 57 (1938)
  - V. I. Shestakov, Algebra of Two-Terminal Circuits Constructed Exclusively of Two-Terminal Components (Algebra of A-Circuits), Avtomatika i Telemekhanika 6(2) (1941), 15–24
  - Charles Petzold, Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software (1999)
